opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the starting point for me is that the dominant framing in alignment has often been something like "align the AI to the user's preferences," or "align it to human values" in some aggregate sense. And both of those run into trouble once you imagine a world with many AI systems, each acting on behalf of different people or organizations whose goals genuinely conflict.

If every assistant is just maximizing its principal's preferences, you've basically recreated all the problems of unconstrained self-interested agents, but now operating faster and at scale. On the other hand, trying to align everything to one global utility function, some aggregate of everyone's values, seems both philosophically fraught and practically impossible. People disagree deeply about what's good, and I don't think we should want, or could ever get, consensus on a single objective.

What humans actually do, though, is something in between. We pursue our own diverse ends, but we do so within a shared structure of norms: conventions, social rules, laws, contracts, expectations about what's permissible. You don't have to agree with me about what makes a life go well for us both to agree that you shouldn't lie to me in a negotiation, or that you queue for the bus, or that you don't take things that aren't yours. Those norms are what make cooperation possible among people with different values. In a sense they're the solution humanity has found to the pluralism problem.

So the proposal is that AI systems should be aligned not just to their principals, but to the normative constraints of the communities they operate in. They should pursue the goals of the people they serve, but only within the bounds of what's mutually agreed to be acceptable. That's what I'd call a contractualist approach to alignment, in contrast to a purely preference-based one.

Then the "learning" part matters because these norms are mostly not written down. Many are implicit, context-dependent, and vary across communities and change over time. You can't just hardcode a list of rules. But humans are remarkably good at inferring norms from relatively few observations, partly because we understand *why* norms exist, what cooperative function they serve. So a lot of my work looks at how you could build agents that infer norms the way people do, through something like Bayesian inference over which norms are in effect, using observed behavior and an understanding of the purposes norms serve, rather than just imitating surface behavior.

There's also a robustness argument. If an agent understands a norm as a constraint shared with others, rather than as one more term in a reward function, it's less tempted to trade off violating the norm for a bit more reward for its principal. Constraints have a different structure from preferences, and I think that structure is precisely what we want when many agents with different masters share one world.

r001.rationale: It says self-interested AI agents would recreate problems at scale, but does not clearly state that their actions impose costs on the rest of society.

r002.rationale: It says norms are mostly unwritten, implicit, context-dependent, and changing, so they cannot simply be hardcoded in advance.

r003.rationale: It proposes inferring norms from observed behavior in communities, using Bayesian inference and an understanding of their purpose.

r004.rationale: It rejects a single global objective and proposes that systems pursue their principals’ goals within shared normative constraints.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that I think the dominant framing of alignment, where we try to get an AI system to learn and optimize for someone's preferences or values, doesn't scale well once you have many AI systems acting on behalf of many different principals who don't agree with each other.

If I build an assistant that's really good at advancing my interests, and you build one that's really good at advancing yours, and we each just maximize, then what we've done is import all the conflicts that exist between humans into a world where the agents acting on those conflicts are much faster and more capable than we are. Preference alignment to individuals, taken on its own, is almost a recipe for an arms race.

So what actually holds human societies together, given that people disagree about values all the time? I'd argue it's mostly not shared values in some deep sense. It's shared norms. We have rules, conventions, laws, and more informal expectations that are mutually recognized, and that constrain what you're allowed to do in pursuit of your goals, even when you and I want very different things. You can pursue your interests, but you can't lie to me in a contract, you can't take my stuff, you can't cut in line. Those constraints are what make cooperation possible among agents who don't share an objective function.

The claim, then, is that if we want AI systems to be deployed on behalf of lots of different individuals and organizations, the thing to get right is less "what does this particular user value" and more "what are the norms that all of these agents, regardless of who they work for, should respect." And crucially, these norms have to be learnable. We can't write them all down by hand. Human normative systems are enormously rich and context dependent, and a lot of what we expect from each other is tacit. So the research question becomes: how does an agent infer, from observing how people behave and how they react to violations, what the operative norms in a given context are? That's a kind of inverse problem, a bit like inverse reinforcement learning, but the target is a system of constraints rather than a reward function.

There are a few reasons I find this framing attractive beyond the scaling argument. One is that norms are often much easier to agree on than values. Two people can have totally incompatible views about what the good life is and still agree that you shouldn't deceive each other. That's roughly the insight behind a lot of contractualist and liberal political philosophy, and I think it transfers. Another is that constraints are more robust than objectives. If I give a system an objective and it's slightly wrong, the system will push hard in a wrong direction. If I give it a constraint and it's slightly wrong, the worst case is usually that it's a bit too conservative. That asymmetry matters a lot when you're uncertain, which we always are.

And a third reason is that it keeps humans in the loop in the right way. Norms are things we collectively negotiate and revise. If AI systems are learning the norms we actually hold, rather than trying to extrapolate some idealized value function, then the legitimacy of what they're doing traces back to actual human institutions and agreements, not to a model's guess about what we'd want on reflection. I think that's a much healthier relationship to be in with these systems.

r001.rationale: It says individually aligned agents would import human conflicts into a world of faster, more capable agents, creating an arms race.

r002.rationale: It says norms are too rich, context dependent, and tacit to write down fully in advance.

r003.rationale: It proposes inferring operative norms by observing people’s behavior and their reactions to violations.

r004.rationale: It presents pursuing a principal’s interests subject to shared norms, but does not frame this as an alternative to finding an optimal plan that satisfies every agent’s preferences.

astra-6.text:
Well, if we have AI systems acting on behalf of different people and organizations, those people are going to want different things. So alignment can’t just mean that each system gets better at satisfying its particular user’s preferences. Those preferences can conflict, and pursuing them can impose costs on everybody else.

Shared normative constraints give us a way to structure that interaction. We don’t have to agree on everything we value to agree that there are certain things we shouldn’t do to one another, or that some actions require consent. Within those constraints, there can still be a lot of room for people to pursue different goals.

And the learning part matters because we can’t expect to write down every relevant constraint in advance. Norms depend on context, and people clarify and revise them as new situations arise. We want systems that can learn from those processes, recognize uncertainty about what’s permissible, and ask for clarification when appropriate.

Of course, learning what people commonly do isn’t the same as learning what’s justified. People can behave badly, and existing norms can be unfair. So this approach needs room for criticism and revision, especially from the people affected. But I think it gives us a useful way to frame alignment as more than a relationship between one AI and one user. It’s also about whether all of these systems can act on our behalf while respecting the claims we have on one another.

r001.rationale: It says agents’ differing preferences can conflict and pursuing them can impose costs on everybody else.

r002.rationale: It states that not every relevant constraint can be written down in advance.

r003.rationale: It proposes systems learning from processes in which people clarify and revise shared norms.

r004.rationale: It allows people to pursue different goals within shared constraints, but does not clearly frame that as an alternative to finding an optimal plan that satisfies every agent’s preferences.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if we have AI systems acting on behalf of different people and organizations, those people are going to want different things. And even if each AI is very good at helping its own user, that doesn’t automatically mean that their interactions will go well. A system could advance its user’s interests in ways that harm other people, violate their rights, or undermine the institutions that make cooperation possible.

So I think we need to distinguish between the goals an agent pursues and the constraints on how it pursues them. We don’t all have to share the same goals to agree that there are certain things we shouldn’t do to one another. Shared normative constraints give us a way to accommodate that diversity while still making it possible for agents to coexist and cooperate.

The learning part matters because those constraints are difficult to specify completely in advance. They depend on context, and people can disagree about how they apply. So we’d like systems that can learn from human judgments and practices, recognize uncertainty, and ask for clarification when appropriate.

And that isn’t just about learning whatever behavior is most common. People routinely violate their own norms. The challenge is to learn what people understand as permissible or obligatory, and to make that understanding open to correction. I see that as one component of alignment: helping an AI serve its user while remaining accountable to the other people affected by its actions.

r001.rationale: It says an agent can advance its user’s interests in ways that harm other people or undermine cooperative institutions.

r002.rationale: It states that normative constraints are difficult to specify completely in advance and depend on context.

r003.rationale: It proposes learning from human judgments and practices to understand what people consider permissible or obligatory.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes shared constraints from shared goals, but does not present this approach as an alternative to finding a plan that satisfies every agent’s preferences.
